extracted.intended_audience: investors, students, securities lawyers, and general readers interested in U.S. securities/takeover law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and disclosure requirements under the Williams Act (1968 amendments to the Securities Exchange Act of 1934) governing cash tender offers and acquisitions of equity in U.S. registered corporations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory disclosure for cash tender offers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Williams Act requires any person who makes a cash tender offer ... to disclose to the federal Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) the source of the funds used in the offer, the purpose for which the offer is made, the plans the purchaser might have if successful, and any contracts or understandings concerning the target corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing and public disclosures with the SEC are required; copies of these disclosure statements must also be sent to each national securities exchange where the securities are traded, making the information available to shareholders and investors. The statute's stated purpose is to require full and fair disclosure for the benefit of stockholders while providing offeror and management equal opportunity to present their cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5% ownership filing threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing and public disclosures with the SEC are also required of anyone who acquires more than 5 percent of the outstanding shares of any class of a corporation subject to federal registration requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This triggers duty to disclose the acquiring person's identity and relevant information; exchange copies must be sent to national securities exchanges where the securities trade so shareholders and investors can access the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on false, misleading, or incomplete statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The law imposes a broad prohibition against the use of false, misleading, or incomplete statements in connection with a tender offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SEC is given authority to institute enforcement lawsuits to address such violations; this functions as both a disclosure and anti-fraud standard in tender offer communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive restrictions on tender offer mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: The law imposes miscellaneous substantive restrictions on the mechanics of a cash tender offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wikipedia article does not exhaustively list these mechanical rules, but indicates the Act regulates offer procedures (timing, amendments, withdrawal rights, etc. in practice) in addition to disclosure duties, and gives the SEC enforcement power over those mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and typical structure of a cash tender offer
rubrics_metrics.description: A tender offer is a proposal to buy shares of stock from the stockholders for cash or some type of corporate security of the acquiring company; a cash tender offer is usually 15-20% in excess of the current market price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts cash tender offers (favored since the mid-1960s for corporate takeovers) with proxy campaigns (attempts to obtain shareholder votes). This contextualizes why disclosure rules were implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to corporations required to be federally registered
rubrics_metrics.description: The Williams Act applies to tender offers for a corporation that is required to be registered under federal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the Act's disclosure and filing duties specifically target transactions involving issuers subject to federal registration requirements (i.e., publicly traded companies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: full and fair disclosure and parity between offeror and management
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the Williams Act is to require full and fair disclosure for the benefit of stockholders, while at the same time providing the offeror and management equal opportunity to fairly present their cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy objective underlies the Act's disclosure duties, exchange-copy requirement, and anti-misleading-statement prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage ambiguity regarding derivatives and non-stock instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: As complicated forms of derivatives bearing upon but not actually constituting corporate stock have become common, interpretation of the Williams Act has become tricky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes this issue came to a head in 2008 in litigation involving CSX Corporation, indicating that whether certain derivative positions trigger Williams Act disclosure or tender-offer rules may be contested and fact-specific.
